name: Beef, salt and water diet

lead: This is a strict elimination-style version of the carnivore diet in which a person eats only beef or other ruminant meat, salt and water. It is often called the lion diet. It became widely known through Mikhaila Peterson and her father Jordan Peterson, who described following it.
Proponents describe it as a way to identify food sensitivities and to relieve autoimmune and mood symptoms. These accounts are anecdotal; no controlled trial has tested the diet.

paras: Advocates say removing all plant foods and most other animal foods eliminates potential triggers such as plant compounds. Near-zero carbohydrate intake means the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis.

Critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation and, with high red-meat intake, associations with colon cancer and gout. Grokipedia notes that early fatigue and cramps usually fade within weeks and that scurvy has been documented in a meat-only case.

lead: The beef, salt and water diet is the strictest form of the carnivore diet, limiting intake to ruminant meat (mostly beef), salt and water.[1][2] It is commonly called the lion diet.[1]

Grokipedia reports that Mikhaila Peterson created the lion diet in 2017 as an elimination protocol for autoimmune arthritis and depression, and Wikipedia reports that she and her father Jordan Peterson publicly followed it, after which it became a viral social-media trend.[1][2] Proponents rely largely on self-reports; the evidence base is described as very low quality, with no large randomised trials.[2]
infobox: Lion diet created 2017 as an elimination protocol (per Grokipedia)

paras: The diet is a minimalist subset of the carnivore diet, which allows only animal products and excludes plants.[1] In its strict form it contains ruminant meat, salt and water and nothing else, and it is designed by its proponents as an elimination protocol to identify sensitivities.[2] Looser versions add poultry, fish, eggs or low-lactose dairy.[2]

Earlier meat-heavy regimens include the 1856 book of Bernard Moncriff, the 1870s diabetes diets of Arnaldo Cantani and James H. Salisbury's 1880s lean beef and hot water diet.[1] Grokipedia also points to Vilhjalmur Stefansson's medically observed meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital in 1928 and 1929 as a key historical reference.[2]
The lion diet reached wide audiences through the Petersons and was covered by outlets including The Guardian and The Atlantic, according to Wikipedia's references.[1]

Advocates claim relief of autoimmune, digestive, skin and mood problems, attributing this to removal of plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates; Grokipedia describes these claims as largely anecdotal.[2] A 2021 survey of 2,029 carnivore dieters found that 95 percent reported overall improvement, but Grokipedia stresses the sample was self-selected and unvalidated.[2]

Nutrition professionals describe the carnivore diet as a fad diet; the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia are among bodies that classify it that way.[1] Cited concerns include lack of dietary fibre, vitamin deficiencies from excluding fruit and vegetables, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, and links between high red-meat intake and colon cancer, gout and kidney strain.[1]

Grokipedia lists possible shortfalls of vitamin C, folate, magnesium, potassium, calcium, thiamin and iodine, a documented scurvy case in a man eating mostly canned beef, and protein toxicity (rabbit starvation) with very lean meat. It also describes transient early fatigue and cramps ('carnivore flu') attributed to electrolyte loss.[2]
No studies found. No controlled trial has tested a beef, salt and water diet. Related evidence for the wider carnivore diet consists of a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.[2]

lore.intro: Communities and media describe the diet as an elimination protocol and as an extreme carnivore challenge.[1][2]

claims.claim: Eating only beef, salt and water resolves autoimmune and mood problems.
Humans do not need plant foods.
